feedback: If a child writes 1/5 for one red among six: recount the whole set aloud including the red — the bottom number is every counter that could be drawn (6), not just the others (5).
If a child swaps to 6/1 or puts the total on top: a probability is never bigger than 1, so the whole (total) sits on the bottom and the favourable part on top.
When the counters change and both the fraction and marker move, name it: 'The symbol and its position on the scale moved together.'
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the total number of equally likely outcomes (every counter that could be drawn), not the count of the OTHER outcomes; the fraction has a size you can locate between 0 and 1.
learnerActions: Fill a bag with coloured counters that are identical apart from colour, which you can see and count, and that will be drawn without looking — e.g. drop in one red among six total.
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction: count the favourable (reds) for the numerator and the WHOLE set (all counters, red included) for the denominator, giving 1/6.
Mark that fraction on a 0-to-1 line (1/6 hugging 0, 1/2 at the middle).
Add more reds and re-count: watch the fraction change and the marker slide up the line together.
Deliberately test the wrong answer: try to make it 1/5 (red to the other five) and re-count the total to see the denominator counts all six counters, not the leftovers.
activities.title: Build the fraction from a bag, and place it on the 0-to-1 line

feedback: If the child writes 3/2 or 3:2: recount the whole set aloud including the reds — the denominator is every counter that could be drawn (5), so the total goes on the bottom, not the leftovers (2).
If the child answers with a raw count ('3'): a probability is always a part of the whole, written as a fraction (or decimal/percent) between 0 and 1, never a plain count.
P(red) and P(not red) together should make 1 (whole bag); use this to check the fraction (here 3/5 and 2/5).
For 26/52: counting 26 favourable of 52 total gives the same value as 1/2 — the equivalent fraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Building the fraction from a NEW situation — not reading a prepared one — is where part-whole understanding shows: a part-whole reasoner writes 3/5, a part-part reasoner writes 3/2 or 3:2 (red to non-red).
learnerActions: Take a bag holding 3 red, 1 blue and 1 green counter (5 in total).
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction, forming favourable-over-total: 3/5.
Mark 3/5 on a 0-to-1 scale (a little above the halfway point).
Then write the probability of NOT red and check what the two fractions add up to.
Try another fair case: a bag with three equally represented colours gives P(one colour) = 1/3, marked a little below the halfway point on the scale.
Reduce a case where it applies: a standard 52-card deck has 26 red cards, so P(red) = 26/52 = 1/2 — connect counting outcomes to equivalent fractions.
activities.title: Construct and translate from a fresh situation

feedback: If a child writes a simple fraction for an uneven spinner as if the regions were equal: check first that outcomes are equally likely; if they aren't, the colour counts are not the counts of equally likely outcomes, so favourable/total does not apply directly.
activities.intendedInsight: favourable/total gives the probability only when the outcomes are equally likely; otherwise the counts of colours/regions are not counts of equally likely outcomes.
learnerActions: Before writing favourable/total, ask: are all the outcomes equally likely?
Compare a fair die or a bag of identical counters (equally likely) with an uneven spinner whose regions differ in size (not equally likely).
For the uneven case, notice why counting colours or regions does not directly give the probability.
activities.title: Check the outcomes are equally likely before counting

feedback: Catch a part-part answer and ask the child to recount the whole set.

For the 3 red, 1 blue, 1 green bag: if they say adding two greens doesn't change anything, the total (denominator) grows from 5 to 7 while the reds (numerator) stay at 3, so the probability of red falls from 3/5 to 3/7.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating that the denominator counts the whole set of equally likely outcomes consolidates part-whole reasoning.
learnerActions: Answer a prompt such as 'What goes on the bottom of the fraction, and why?'
If you give a part-part answer, re-count the whole set and explain which outcomes the denominator includes.
Using your 3 red, 1 blue, 1 green bag, explain whether adding two more green counters would change the probability of red, and which number in your fraction changes.
activities.title: Talk it through: why that number on the bottom?
